account: GiveDirectly's MobileAid approach uses machine learning on mobile-phone usage patterns to identify people in need and pay them by mobile money. GiveDirectly says that it has evaluated the method across four countries since 2021 (Togo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Malawi and Bangladesh). In Malawi it ran a Canva-funded pilot in Khongoni, in rural Lilongwe, and GiveDirectly says that the pilot launched in March 2022. A World Bank discussion paper by Yuko Okamura, Tim Ohlenburg and Emil Tesliuc (March 2024) describes the pilot. Drawing on GiveDirectly's internal data, the authors report that 3,052 of 12,800 recipients were chosen with phone data and that the hybrid approach cost about half as much per added enrollee as in-person surveys alone. They also judge that the phone model did only slightly better than random choice when most people were eligible. GiveDirectly's 27 January 2025 post (Nirali Desai and Vera Lummis) describes interviews with 67 recipients across Malawi and Kenya in February and October 2024. The interviews, which name Mzuzu, asked how to explain targeting by AI and machine learning. The authors found that scenario-based explanations were the most understandable. GiveDirectly's 4 September 2025 post (Vera Lummis) says that in Malawi it ran a hybrid program that identified and enrolled 35% of recipients via phone metadata and 65% in person. That share differs from the World Bank count of 3,052 of 12,800 recipients. The post says that the hybrid halved the cost of identifying and enrolling each additional person compared with a fully in-person operation, and it links that claim to the World Bank paper. GiveDirectly says that it is working with the Government of Malawi to fill gaps in the urban social registry with phone metadata. A study with the Government of Malawi, U.C. Berkeley and U.C. San Diego is expected to report in 2026. It asks whether phone metadata can flag people whose poverty deepens after a shock.

ai_role.statement: In the Khongoni pilot a machine-learning model scored phone records to estimate consumption, and people below the cutoff could enroll by USSD; 3,052 of the 12,800 recipients joined this way, within 56 hours of ID validation. GiveDirectly staff then surveyed the same villages door to door to enroll people the phone method missed. The World Bank authors credit the hybrid with halving the variable enrollment cost. They also report GiveDirectly's estimates of 17% targeting error for the model against 13% for the in-person test, and they judge that the model did little better than random choice at the 80% cutoff.

fields.account: GiveDirectly's MobileAid approach uses machine learning on mobile-phone usage patterns to identify people in need and pay them by mobile money. GiveDirectly says that it has evaluated the method across four countries since 2021 (Togo, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Malawi and Bangladesh). In Malawi it ran a Canva-funded pilot in Khongoni, in rural Lilongwe, and GiveDirectly says that the pilot launched in March 2022. A World Bank discussion paper by Yuko Okamura, Tim Ohlenburg and Emil Tesliuc (March 2024) describes the pilot. Drawing on GiveDirectly's internal data, the authors report that 3,052 of 12,800 recipients were chosen with phone data and that the hybrid approach cost about half as much per added enrollee as in-person surveys alone. They also judge that the phone model did only slightly better than random choice when most people were eligible. GiveDirectly's 27 January 2025 post (Nirali Desai and Vera Lummis) describes interviews with 67 recipients across Malawi and Kenya in February and October 2024. The interviews, which name Mzuzu, asked how to explain targeting by AI and machine learning. The authors found that scenario-based explanations were the most understandable. GiveDirectly's 4 September 2025 post (Vera Lummis) says that in Malawi it ran a hybrid program that identified and enrolled 35% of recipients via phone metadata and 65% in person. That share differs from the World Bank count of 3,052 of 12,800 recipients. The post says that the hybrid halved the cost of identifying and enrolling each additional person compared with a fully in-person operation, and it links that claim to the World Bank paper. GiveDirectly says that it is working with the Government of Malawi to fill gaps in the urban social registry with phone metadata. A study with the Government of Malawi, U.C. Berkeley and U.C. San Diego is expected to report in 2026. It asks whether phone metadata can flag people whose poverty deepens after a shock.
